channel.title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Power
channel.description: Curated OT/ICS advisories, incidents and threat intelligence. Editorial by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

item.title: [Critical] PHP2Shell is in KEV and being exploited against internet-facing PAN-OS firewall management, and Siemens lists RUGGEDCOM APE1808 as affected
item.category: Top Story
item.description: CISA added both PHP2Shell flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS v4.0 9.2, PHP Group), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 26 October with a 29 October federal deadline. Palo Alto Networks’ advisory, raised to Critical on 27 October and updated again on 28 October, reports active exploitation targeting PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. PAN-OS on PA-Series and VM-Series firewalls and on Panorama is affected through the management web interface and XML API; GlobalProtect is not. Palo Alto’s own 9.2 score falls to 5.2 when management access is limited to a jump box. Hotfixes are rolling out train by train, with the last few due 29–30 October, and Palo Alto says they also fix the Brotli decoder flaw that CISA added to KEV on 27 October. Siemens’ SSA-566512 (23 October) lists RUGGEDCOM APE1808 running any PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1 or 12.2 release as affected; customers obtain fixes through Siemens support and should apply Palo Alto’s workarounds meanwhile. Researchers at Perplexity, with Expel’s Marcus Hutchins concurring, confirmed working remote code execution against a honeypot over 24–25 October. No victim organisation has been named, CISA did not describe the activity, and no exploitation of an APE1808 has been reported. Siemens describes the APE1808 as a utility-grade platform for running security applications in harsh industrial settings, so it is often the boundary firewall at substations and field sites (editorial assessment). - Palo Alto Networks advisory for CVE-2026-109618, 21 Oct 2026, raised to Critical 27 Oct and updated 28 Oct; Siemens ProductCERT SSA-566512, 23 Oct 2026; CISA KEV listing, 26 Oct 2026 (primary); Perplexity and Expel findings reported by BleepingComputer and Cybersecurity Dive - PHP fixes 21 Oct 2026; Siemens advisory 23 Oct; KEV-listed 26 Oct; Palo Alto exploitation update 27–28 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Attackers chained Ivanti Connect Secure flaws to take root on fully patched VPNs; one link still has no patch
item.category: Incident — Exploited VPN zero-day chain, CISA KEV; one link still unpatched
item.description: Ivanti disclosed on 13 October that attackers had chained three Connect Secure flaws to gain root on fully patched appliances at a limited number of customers. Two of the flaws are fixed under a single identifier, CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS v3.1 8.6), which CISA added to KEV that day with a 16 October deadline. The third, a privilege escalation, has no CVE and no patch; Ivanti said a fix would follow in the coming weeks. None had appeared publicly by 28 October. Volexity, which found the chain during incident response, tracks the actor as UTA0576, a new actor; exploitation dates to at least early October. The intruders left no web shell: they stole domain credentials, pulled LAPS passwords and BitLocker keys, and wiped logs. Volexity and CISA warn that Ivanti’s Integrity Checker may miss this compromise. No utility victim has been named, but these VPNs often carry staff and vendor access toward control-system networks (editorial assessment). - Ivanti security advisory for CVE-2026-104935 and CISA KEV listing, 13 Oct 2026 (primary); Volexity analysis, 13 Oct 2026; reported by SecurityWeek, CyberScoop and Cybersecurity Dive - Disclosed and KEV-listed 13 Oct 2026; exploited since at least early October

item.title: [Critical] A fourth critical Citrix NetScaler flaw means some appliances patched for the exploited zero-days must be upgraded again
item.category: Incident — Exploited remote-access appliance zero-days, CISA KEV; fourth critical flaw patched
item.description: Citrix published bulletin CTX697191 on 8 October for CVE-2026-107406 (CVSS v4.0 9.5), a memory overflow in NetScaler ADC and Gateway configured as a SAML service provider or identity provider that Citrix says may lead to code execution or denial of service. The builds that fixed the September zero-days stay exposed when the appliance acts as a SAML identity provider, so those customers must upgrade again; there is no workaround. Citrix says it is not aware of exploitation of the new flaw, and it is not in KEV. It lands in the middle of an active campaign: CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 (both CVSS v4 9.5) were exploited before patches existed and entered KEV on 27 September, and CVE-2026-88779, a denial-of-service flaw according to Citrix and watchTowr, followed on 4 October. CISA has warned that attackers use it to force reboots so that code planted through CVE-2026-88771 runs, and has published Sigma detection rules. Mandiant counts dozens of victim organizations and calls the actors suspected state-nexus without naming a group; Arctic Wolf counts at least 78 targeted organizations, and Shadowserver sees more than 20,000 exposed or potentially vulnerable appliances. Intruders planted web shells, and Mandiant warns that upgrading alone does not remove access already gained. No power-sector victim has been named, but NetScaler often fronts contractor and field-staff access at utilities, so an unhunted appliance is a possible first hop toward EMS, SCADA and substation networks (editorial assessment). - Citrix bulletins CTX697191 (8 Oct 2026), CTX697174 and CTX697096; CISA KEV listings 27 Sep and 4 Oct 2026 (primary); Mandiant, Arctic Wolf, watchTowr and Shadowserver findings reported by SecurityWeek, Cybersecurity Dive and The Hacker News - First two flaws KEV-listed 27 Sep 2026; third 4 Oct 2026; fourth flaw disclosed 8 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager authentication bypass CVE-2026-76504 was exploited as a zero-day; there is no workaround
item.category: Incident — Exploited SD-WAN management zero-day, CISA KEV
item.description: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-76504 (CVSS 9.8) on 30 September: Catalyst SD-WAN Manager mishandles URI encoding, so a crafted HTTP request can bypass an API authentication rule and give a remote, unauthenticated attacker administrative access. Cisco says its PSIRT became aware of active exploitation in September, and CISA added the flaw to KEV the same day with a 3 October federal deadline, now passed. Cisco revised the advisory on 2 October. There is no workaround; a temporary Live Protect shield gives partial protection but may block some legitimate users. BleepingComputer counts this as the fifth exploited SD-WAN zero-day of 2026. No actor, victim or sector has been named. SD-WAN Manager pushes policy to the overlay that many utilities use to link offices, plants and substations, so administrative access to it is a position from which traffic paths toward field sites could be changed (editorial assessment). - Cisco security advisory cisco-sa-sdwan-webauth-xr8beuuU, 30 Sep 2026, revised 2 Oct (primary); CISA KEV 30 Sep 2026; reported by BleepingComputer - Disclosed and KEV-listed 30 Sep 2026; advisory v1.1 2 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Arista says a VeloCloud Orchestrator flaw that lets any logged-in user take operator control is being exploited; CISA’s deadline has passed
item.category: Incident — Exploited SD-WAN orchestrator flaw, CISA KEV
item.description: Arista disclosed CVE-2026-114625 in Security Advisory 0199 on 22 October: an SQL injection in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) that lets any authenticated user, down to the Enterprise Read Only role, escalate to operator-level rights by impersonating a built-in superuser account. Arista rates it CVSS v3.1 9.9 and v4.0 9.4, says it found the issue itself and that it is known to be actively exploited, and lists two source IP addresses to block. CISA added the flaw to KEV on 23 October with a 26 October federal deadline, now passed. Releases 5.2.3.18, 6.1.3.10 and 6.4.2.12 fix it; hosted orchestrators, including Dedicated ones, were also affected and Arista has already patched them. Arista notes that the orchestrator’s web interface is exposed by default. No actor, victim or sector has been named. The orchestrator pushes configuration to the SD-WAN edges that link offices, plants and remote sites, so operator access is a position from which paths toward field sites could be changed (editorial assessment). - Arista Security Advisory 0199, 22 Oct 2026; CISA KEV listing, 23 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by Security Affairs and The Hacker News - Disclosed 22 Oct 2026; KEV-listed 23 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Attackers are abusing a signed Siemens Software Center binary in ClickFix attacks; CISA’s patch deadline is 3 November
item.category: Incident — Signed OT-vendor software abused in ClickFix attacks; CISA KEV
item.description: Siemens confirmed on 19 October that CVE-2026-110936, a DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens Software Center, is being exploited in what it calls the Romulus ClickFix campaign. Attackers bundle a genuine, validly signed copy of version 3.5.8.7 with their own DLLs in an installer such as AllMyBasic.msi; when a lured user runs it, the Siemens program loads the attackers’ code. Siemens says no Siemens system, product or update channel was breached, and it names no malware family. The flaw is rated CVSS v3.1 6.7 and v4.0 8.4; version 4.0.9.8 fixes it, and existing installs update on their next start. CISA added it to KEV on 20 October with a 3 November deadline and republished the advisory on 22 October as ICSA-26-295-03, listing the Energy sector. As of 28 October Siemens had not revised SSA-580366 beyond version 1.2 of 19 October, and no new campaign reporting had appeared. No utility victim is known. Because the Siemens file is genuine, Siemens advises detecting by location and behaviour rather than by file hash, and publisher-based allow-listing on engineering workstations may trust it too (editorial assessment). - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-580366 (15 Oct 2026, updated 19 Oct) and exploitation notice, 19 Oct 2026 (primary); CISA KEV listing, 20 Oct 2026, and ICSA-26-295-03, 22 Oct 2026; reported by SecurityWeek and BleepingComputer - Advisory 15 Oct 2026; exploitation confirmed 19 Oct; KEV-listed 20 Oct; CISA republication 22 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA adds the BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, exploited by a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor since late August, to KEV
item.category: Incident — Exploited remote-support zero-day, suspected state espionage; now in CISA KEV
item.description: CISA added CVE-2026-102764, a zero-day in BeyondTrust Remote Support, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 16 October with a 19 October federal deadline. A day earlier Google Threat Intelligence Group said the flaw (CVSS v4.0 9.3) had been exploited from late August; it attributes the activity to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221, based on overlapping tools and techniques. The attackers gained root on Remote Support appliances, harvested credentials, deleted logs and used the product’s file-transfer feature to pull documents from users’ desktops, deploying the SAWFLY web shell and the BARECLAW tunneler. Versions up to 26.2.3 are affected. BeyondTrust identified the defect in late September, shipped patch BT26-05-RS on 8 October and had patched its SaaS customers by 9 October; self-hosted appliances without automatic updates must be patched by hand, and releases older than 24.3.1 must be upgraded first. GTIG names no victims or sectors. Remote-support tools like this are how many OEMs, integrators and help desks reach plant workstations, so the relevance to power operators is the vendor-access path (editorial assessment). - Google Threat Intelligence Group analysis and BeyondTrust advisory BT26-05, 15 Oct 2026; CISA KEV listing, 16 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by SecurityWeek - Exploited from late August 2026; fix released 8 Oct 2026; disclosed 15 Oct 2026; KEV-listed 16 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] The FortiOS flaw behind Unit 42’s Peerstitch intrusion is now in KEV, and its CVE record also lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808
item.category: Incident — Exploited firewall-management chain at a telecom MSP; FortiOS flaw added to CISA KEV
item.description: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 reported on 14 October that an intruder at a telecommunications managed service provider exploited the FortiManager flaw CVE-2024-47575 (“FortiJump”), then used CVE-2025-61624, a path traversal in the FortiOS command line, to act as root on managed FortiGates and run PEERSTITCH, a memory-resident injector that opens a covert channel between two FortiOS daemons and leaves no file on disk. Configuration and credential material from more than 500 managed FortiGates was exposed; Unit 42 stresses that this is exposure, not confirmed intrusion into those customers’ networks. It tracks the cluster as CL-STA-0954 (UNC5820) and notes overlap with suspected nation-state intrusions, but names no state. CISA added CVE-2025-61624 to KEV on 16 October with a 19 October deadline. Fortinet rates the flaw Medium because it needs privileged, authenticated access, and fixed it in April. The public CVE record also lists Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808, an application-hosting platform that can run FortiOS, as affected. Utilities that let an MSP manage boundary firewalls through FortiManager share this kind of exposure (editorial assessment). - Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 report, 14 Oct 2026; Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-122; CISA KEV listing, 16 Oct 2026 (primary); CVE record via CIRCL; reported by The Hacker News - Unit 42 report 14 Oct 2026; KEV-listed 16 Oct 2026; Fortinet fix April 2026

item.title: [High] FBI and Secret Service: FortiBleed credential theft against FortiGate VPNs is still active, and energy is among the targeted sectors
item.category: Incident — Active credential-theft campaign against firewall and VPN gateways; no CVE
item.description: The FBI and US Secret Service warned on 6 October that the FortiBleed campaign against internet-facing Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways is still active. There is no CVE: the agencies say attackers exploit reused or leaked credentials and legacy SHA-256 password storage, and researchers describe credential stuffing and spraying, offline hash cracking and a sniffer that captures authentication traffic. Intruders create their own administrator accounts and sometimes delete or reset the real ones, locking owners out, and the access is resold; the FBI advisory links it to Payload ransomware, and SOCRadar says it has confirmed at least 12 ransomware deployments from it. SOCRadar’s figure of 86,644 working device credentials across 194 countries dates from 19 June; it is not a new count. The agencies say targets span all 16 US critical-infrastructure sectors, including energy. No compromise of an OT system has been described, but FortiGates commonly sit at the IT/OT boundary and in front of remote access to plants and substations (editorial assessment). - FBI and US Secret Service joint advisory JCSA-20261006-01, 6 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by Cybersecurity Dive and The Hacker News - Warning issued 6 Oct 2026; credential count dates from 19 Jun 2026

item.title: [High] Fortinet FortiMail flaw CVE-2026-104286 was exploited before a fix existed; Fortinet’s 5 October update now lists fixed releases
item.category: Incident — Exploited email-security gateway zero-day, CISA KEV
item.description: Fortinet published advisory FG-IR-26-175 on 1 October for CVE-2026-104286 (CVSS 9.8), a path-traversal flaw in FortiMail that lets an unauthenticated attacker write arbitrary files on the appliance with crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests. Fortinet says the flaw has been reported exploited in the wild, and CISA added it to KEV on 1 October with a 4 October deadline. No fixed build was available at disclosure; Fortinet’s 5 October update lists 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9, and tells 7.2 users to move to the 7.4 branch or later. Fortinet still urges its workarounds: turn off the IBE feature, restrict the webmail interface to trusted networks, and block POST requests to /ibe paths that contain “../”. No actor or victims have been disclosed. FortiMail sits on the corporate side rather than in control networks, but a compromised mail gateway is a trusted platform for phishing operations and engineering staff (editorial assessment). - Fortinet PSIRT advisory FG-IR-26-175, 1 Oct 2026, updated 5 Oct (primary); CISA KEV 1 Oct 2026; reported by SecurityWeek - Disclosed and KEV-listed 1 Oct 2026; fixed releases listed 5 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] CenterPoint Energy’s breach reached more than 1 million Texans, its state filing shows; the company reports no operational impact
item.category: Incident — Confirmed customer-data breach at a US electric & gas utility; scope update
item.description: CenterPoint Energy has told the Texas Attorney General’s Office that 1,062,060 Texas residents were affected by the breach it disclosed in September, with names, addresses, Social Security numbers and driver’s license numbers exposed, SecurityWeek reported on 15 October. Residents of Indiana, Minnesota and Ohio may also be affected, and the overall total is not yet clear. CenterPoint says the incident did not affect its operations. In its 15 September SEC filing the company said an unauthorized third party obtained customer personal information through an externally facing system, and that it learned of the breach from the actor’s own public post: a 2.5 GB archive offered on 12 September with a claim of about 7.5 million records and a threat to attack “the main infrastructure” next. The entry point and the actor remain undisclosed, and the 7.5 million figure is unconfirmed. This is an IT-side data breach, not an OT compromise, but stolen identity data is raw material for phishing and social engineering against utility staff and customers. - CenterPoint Energy filing with the Texas Attorney General’s Office, reported by SecurityWeek; CenterPoint SEC filing, 15 Sep 2026 (primary) - Data posted for sale 12 Sep 2026; SEC disclosure 15 Sep 2026; Texas figure reported 15 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] Engie says attackers took French customers’ contact and supply-point details from a partner marketing tool; its own systems were not breached
item.category: Incident — Customer-data breach at a partner marketing tool; no operational impact
item.description: In customer notices reported on 27 October, Engie said it had found unusual data access in a tool that its business partners use to prospect for customers and market energy offers in France. It cut off the access, says the incident is limited to customers in France, and says its internal IT systems were not compromised. The notification letters list names, postal and email addresses, phone numbers, the PDL or PCE supply-point identifier, customer ID and contract number; Engie says no banking data was involved. It has not said how many customers were affected or when the access began, no group has claimed the breach, and no operational impact has been reported. This is a third-party, IT-side breach, but real supply-point and contract numbers make utility-themed phishing far more convincing (editorial assessment). - Engie statement and customer notification letters, reported by BleepingComputer (27 Oct 2026) and Infosecurity Magazine (28 Oct 2026) - Disclosed 27 Oct 2026; further coverage 28 Oct 2026; detection date not disclosed

item.title: [High] FBI seizes domains behind China-linked scanning and phishing tools whose targets included a US power company
item.category: Threat Intelligence — US seizure of China-linked scanning and phishing infrastructure; a US power company among named targets
item.description: On 8 October the Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorized seizures of domains used to run Microscan, a Python web application with more than 1,300 penetration-testing scripts, and FishHub, a spear-phishing and malware-delivery platform. US authorities say both were built and run by China-based Integrity Technology Group, the company sanctioned last year and tied to a 2024 botnet takedown; CyberScoop calls the tools Flax Typhoon-linked, while Cybersecurity Dive says the activity mimics the group tracked as Flax Typhoon. A Mirai-variant IoT botnet supported Microscan. Court documents list Microscan targets including a South Carolina power company, gas and power companies in Taiwan, airports in Japan and Poland and a multinational NGO; FishHub was used against Taiwanese universities. No compromise of the power company or the Taiwanese utilities has been confirmed. A joint FBI, CISA and NSA advisory accompanies the action, and CISA’s Chris Butera said China-affiliated actors keep positioning themselves inside critical-infrastructure networks, OT systems included. - DOJ/FBI domain seizures and joint FBI/CISA/NSA advisory, 8 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by CyberScoop and Cybersecurity Dive - Announced 8 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] Insurer Resilience: ransomware is 9% of energy and utility claims but about 70% of losses, and no claim involved control-system manipulation
item.category: Research — Insurer claims data from energy and utility clients, 2023–2026
item.description: Cyber insurer Resilience has analysed claims filed by its energy and utility clients between January 2023 and early September 2026, Industrial Cyber reported on 21 October. Ransomware made up about 9% of the sector’s claims, against 6% across the rest of its portfolio, yet drove roughly 70% of incurred losses. Email compromise was the most frequent cause at 21% of claims but only about 2% of losses, and 17% of claims began at a vendor, about a third of them HR, payroll, benefits or accounting firms. None of the energy claims, water and wastewater clients included, involved manipulation of a control system; Resilience says that probably understates OT risk, because intrusions can go unnoticed. Attackers got past MFA by socially engineering one-time codes and hijacking sessions, and tested backups and segmentation let some clients recover or keep production running. This is one insurer’s book of business, not a census of the sector. - Resilience, “Cyber risk in energy and utilities: Lessons from Insurance Claims”, reported by Industrial Cyber - Reported 21 Oct 2026; claims filed 1 Jan 2023 – 5 Sep 2026

item.title: [Low] Nozomi telemetry: energy, utilities and waste rose to third for OT alerts per organization this summer
item.category: Research — Vendor OT/IoT telemetry for June–August 2026
item.description: Nozomi Networks Labs’ review of June–August 2026 telemetry from its customers ranks manufacturing first for alerts per organization and transportation second, with energy, utilities and waste moving up to third in place of government. Credential-related techniques made up roughly a third of detections. Among alerts it could tie to an actor, Nozomi attributes close to half to Scattered Spider, and Russia-linked or Russian-speaking actors together account for more than a third. Siemens PLCs and Rockwell products were among the most-detected vulnerable products, and Nozomi says 58% of this year’s vulnerabilities rate High or Critical, against 48% in 2025. These are alert counts from Nozomi’s own sensors, not confirmed intrusions, and the ranking reflects its customer base. - Nozomi Networks Labs blog, 12 Oct 2026 (primary) - Published 12 Oct 2026

item.title: [Critical] Critical unauthenticated code-execution flaw in GPA’s openPDC and openHistorian grid-data software; fixes are out
item.category: Advisory — Synchrophasor data concentrator and historian, unauthenticated remote code execution, no known exploitation
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-281-02, published 8 October, covers the Grid Protection Alliance’s open-source openPDC phasor data concentrator and openHistorian time-series historian. The most serious flaw, CVE-2026-100730 (CVSS v3.1 9.8, v4.0 9.3), is a deserialization bug in the service console: where Windows Authentication is not in use, an unauthenticated attacker on the network can reach it and run code as the service account. Other flaws in the advisory leave data publishers without authentication in default configurations, exposing topology information and STTP data exchange: CVE-2026-105281 (v3.1 7.5) and CVE-2026-85479 (v3.1 5.3). openPDC 2.9.482 and openHistorian 2.8.585 fix them; the Docker image is not fixed. New installs bind publishers to the loopback interface, but upgraded installs keep their old binding and must be checked by hand. CISA reports no known exploitation. These servers sit between substation phasor measurements and control-center analytics, so a compromised one is a foothold between networks (editorial assessment). - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-281-02 and CVE records issued by CISA as CNA (primary); CISA bulletin of six ICS advisories - Published 8 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] PHP2Shell in OT software: Schneider now has a fix for EcoStruxure Control Engineering, ABB has APROL patches scheduled, and Siemens and Rockwell list products not affected
item.category: Advisory — Exploited PHP flaws in OT engineering and security software; Schneider remediation now available
item.description: With both PHP2Shell flaws now in KEV (see the top story), the OT software that bundles PHP needs the same attention as the firewalls. Schneider Electric updated SESB-2026-295-01 to version 2.0.0 on 26 October to say that remediation is now available for EcoStruxure Control Engineering: it installs automatically when the virtual machine can reach the debian.org and sury.org repositories, and sites without that access can request a patch from Schneider support. EcoStruxure Security Expert is fixed in 1.48.4.0, and LINEoptimize (formerly ProLeiT Plant iT LMS) customers go through ProLeiT support. ABB’s B&R unit lists APROL up to R 4.4-65 as affected in SA26P015 (23 October), with patches planned for 26 and 29 October; we could not confirm they have shipped. ABB’s 4HZK000017 tells ABB MES sites running DokuWiki to update PHP or shut DokuWiki down. ABB scores both flaws 9.8 under CVSS v3.1. Rockwell Automation’s SD1802 (23 October) has confirmed no affected products while its review continues. Siemens lists 31 software products in SSA-566435 and 20 Smart Infrastructure products in SSA-166980 as not affected and says its evaluation is ongoing. Moxa has published a response, MPSA-260001. A third PHP flaw, CVE-2026-115560, has only a configuration mitigation and is not reported exploited. No exploitation of any of these OT products has been reported. Engineering and security servers with a built-in web interface are easy to miss in patch inventories (editorial assessment). - Schneider Electric SESB-2026-295-01 v2.0.0, 26 Oct 2026; ABB/B&R SA26P015 and ABB 4HZK000017, 23 Oct 2026; Rockwell Automation SD1802, 23 Oct 2026; Siemens ProductCERT SSA-566435 (23 Oct) and SSA-166980 (26 Oct); Moxa MPSA-260001, 22 Oct 2026 (primary); CISA KEV, 26 Oct 2026 - Vendor notices 22–23 Oct 2026; Schneider remediation, Siemens SSA-166980 and KEV listing 26 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] CISA’s 20 October ICS batch: root command injection in WAGO controllers, a hard-coded key in a Moxa edge gateway and revised Hitachi Energy grid advisories
item.category: Advisory — CISA ICS advisories of 20 October: controller command injection, edge-gateway hard-coded key, revised Hitachi Energy advisories; no known exploitation
item.description: CISA released five ICS advisories on 20 October; four matter most to grid operators. ICSA-26-293-02 republishes WAGO’s advisory for CC100, PFC100 G2, PFC200 G2, TP600, Edge Controller and WP400 devices on firmware before 4.10.0 (FW32): CVE-2026-80466 (CVSS v3.1 8.8) lets a low-privileged remote user inject commands through the web-management routing settings, which a root helper then runs, and CVE-2026-88850 (v3.1 8.1) lets such a user change root-owned PROFIBUS parameters; firmware 4.10.0 fixes both. ICSA-26-293-03 covers Moxa’s AIG-302 edge gateway with ThingsPro Edge 1.4.0 and earlier: a hard-coded cryptographic key, CVE-2026-109813 (v3.1 8.1, v4.0 8.6), and a missing-authorization flaw, CVE-2026-109812 (v3.1 6.8); version 1.4.1 fixes them. CISA also issued third revisions of two Hitachi Energy advisories first published on 1 September: MicroSCADA X SYS600, where CVE-2026-9853 and CVE-2026-9854 (v3.1 7.8, v4.0 8.5) allow authentication bypass and escalation to Windows administrator (fixed in 10.8), and RTU500 CMU firmware, whose nine flaws peak at CVE-2026-6653 (v3.1 8.8) and are fixed in 13.9.1 or 12.7.8. CISA did not say what changed in the revisions, and the RTU500 item is separate from the end-of-life RTU500 firmware advisory in this section. All four list the Energy sector; none is reported exploited. - CISA ICS advisories ICSA-26-293-02 to -05, 20 Oct 2026, republishing WAGO (VDE-2026-096), Moxa and Hitachi Energy advisories (primary); CSAF records via CIRCL - Released 20 Oct 2026; Hitachi Energy originals 1 Sep 2026

item.title: [High] Mitsubishi Electric fixes critical authentication-bypass flaws in ICONICS GENESIS64 and GENESIS; MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz get no fix
item.category: Advisory — SCADA/HMI and historian suite, authentication bypass and permission flaws, no known exploitation; three products get no fix
item.description: Mitsubishi Electric advisory 2026-006, published 15 October, covers ICONICS GENESIS, GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI and IoTWorX, plus MC Works64, GENESIS32 and BizViz. CVE-2026-16436 (CVSS v4.0 9.2) is an authentication bypass: a fixed, shared challenge-response unlocks any user account, although a remote attacker must first obtain that response. CVE-2026-16438 (v4.0 9.4) stems from default DCOM permissions granted to the administrator account, and CVE-2026-16437 (v4.0 7.1) lets an administrator read or write the challenge-response file. The bundled libwebp flaw CVE-2023-4863 (v4.0 9.3) affects GENESIS64 and ICONICS Suite 10.97 to 10.97.2 but needs a local administrator to import a crafted file. Fixes are in ICONICS Suite and IoTWorX 10.98, GENESIS 11.04 and, for libwebp, 10.97.3. There will be no fix for MC Works64, GENESIS32 or BizViz; Mitsubishi tells users to migrate or apply mitigations. No exploitation is reported and none of the flaws is in KEV. CISA republished the advisory on 27 October as ICSA-26-300-02, listing CVSS v3.1 scores of 9.1 for CVE-2026-16438, 8.1 for CVE-2026-16436, 6.4 for CVE-2026-16437 and 8.2 for CVE-2023-4863. ICONICS HMI and historian software is used across energy and utility operations, so these servers often sit close to control networks (editorial assessment). - Mitsubishi Electric PSIRT advisory 2026-006, 15 Oct 2026, and CISA republication ICSA-26-300-02, 27 Oct 2026 (primary) - Published 15 Oct 2026; CISA republication 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] October ICS Patch Tuesday: fixes for Siemens CROSSBOW and Schneider Sage RTUs, but no fix yet for S7-1500 web-server flaws
item.category: Advisory — October ICS Patch Tuesday, grid-relevant items, no known exploitation
item.description: Siemens and Schneider Electric published their October advisories on 13 October; SecurityWeek counts 17 from Siemens. Three matter most to utilities. Siemens SSA-508506 fixes 11 flaws in RUGGEDCOM CROSSBOW, Siemens’ access manager for remote engineering connections to substation devices (our description), including SQL injection and retrieval of administrator credentials, with a top CVSS v3.1 score of 8.8; V6.0 fixes them. Siemens SSA-591731 covers eight web-server flaws in S7-1500, ET 200SP and related CPUs (CVSS v3.1 9.6) that could let an attacker run code in an authorized user’s browser and act on the PLC with that user’s rights; all versions are affected and only mitigations exist. Schneider’s SEVD-2026-286-02 says Sage RTUs (1410, 1430, 1450, 2400, 3030 Magnum and 4400) do not adequately verify firmware authenticity, so modified firmware could be loaded when an administrator starts an update (CVE-2026-102250, v3.1 7.2); firmware C3414-500-S02L0 fixes it. Siemens also updated SSA-794185 on RADIUS (BlastRADIUS) in SIPROTEC and SICAM products, and CISA’s ICSA-26-286-01, which lists the Energy sector, covers an Inductive Automation Ignition privilege escalation (CVE-2026-92817, 8.8; fixed in 8.1.55 and 8.3.9). None is reported exploited or in KEV. CISA republished Siemens’ 13 October advisories on 22 October as ICSA-26-295-02 to -18, and the S7 PLC web-server flaws still have no fix. - Siemens ProductCERT SSA-508506, SSA-591731 and SSA-794185; Schneider Electric SEVD-2026-286-02; CISA ICSA-26-286-01 (primary); SecurityWeek ICS Patch Tuesday roundup - Published 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [High] Unauthenticated firmware upload in end-of-life Hitachi Energy RTU500 firmware; the fix is migration to a supported branch
item.category: Advisory — Substation RTU end-of-life firmware, unauthenticated firmware upload, no known exploitation
item.description: On 6 October CISA republished Hitachi Energy advisory 8DBD000251, first issued on 29 September, as ICSA-26-279-06. It covers six vulnerabilities in end-of-life RTU500 series CMU firmware, 11.x and earlier. The most serious, CVE-2026-8065 (CVSS v3.1 9.1), is missing authentication on the firmware-update endpoint, which lets an unauthenticated attacker upload arbitrary firmware with a crafted request; CVE-2026-8066 (9.1) is an unauthenticated directory traversal in file upload, and the list includes an old VxWorks debug-agent flaw, CVE-2010-2965 (9.8). Dragos reported the findings. Supported firmware is not affected, and Hitachi Energy’s remedy is to move to 12.7.8, 13.9.1 or later. CISA lists the Energy sector and reports no known exploitation. The same batch covered Hitachi Energy Asset Suite, where an unauthenticated test servlet allows configuration upload (CVE-2026-7395, 8.1; fix in 9.9.1 when available), and REB500 busbar protection, whose libexpat flaws are fixed in 8.3.4.0. RTU500s link substations and field sites to the control center, so attacker-supplied firmware on one would put code directly in the telecontrol path (editorial assessment). - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-279-06, republishing Hitachi Energy PSIRT advisory 8DBD000251 (primary); CISA ICSA-26-279-03 and -05 for Asset Suite and REB500 - Hitachi Energy advisory 29 Sep 2026; CISA republication 6 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] WaterISAC: Fortinet has shipped fixes for FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator ahead of a 10 November disclosure
item.category: Advisory — Fortinet fixes released before disclosure; CVE details due 10 November; no exploitation reported
item.description: WaterISAC told members on 27 October that Fortinet has released a coordinated set of updates for critical and high-severity flaws, found through its AI-assisted security testing, in FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator. Fortinet plans to publish the advisories, CVE IDs and CVSS scores on its PSIRT page on 10 November, so until then scanners that rely on CVE data will not flag unpatched devices. Fixed releases, per WaterISAC: FortiOS 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13 and 7.2.14; FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12 and 7.2.13; FortiMail 8.0.2, 7.6.7 and 7.4.9, with 7.2 users moving to 7.4 or later; FortiAuthenticator 8.0.4 and 6.6.11. FortiSASE was updated automatically. WaterISAC reports no exploitation of the undisclosed flaws but warns that attackers can study the published fixes before the details come out. The FortiMail releases also fix CVE-2026-104286, which is already exploited (see Incidents & Attacks). We found no matching Fortinet PSIRT post, so this card rests on WaterISAC’s notice. FortiGates are common at utility IT/OT boundaries and in front of remote access to substations (editorial assessment). - WaterISAC TLP:CLEAR vulnerability notification, 27 Oct 2026; Fortinet advisories due on its PSIRT page 10 Nov 2026 - Notice issued 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] Moxa: its remote-access client can be fooled into trusting a fake server, and the end-of-life OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway gets no fix
item.category: Advisory — Remote-access client and end-of-life cellular gateway flaws; no fix for the gateway; no known exploitation
item.description: Moxa published MPSA-269510 on 27 October. CVE-2026-111459 (CVSS v4.0 7.6) affects the client for Moxa Remote Connect Suite (MRC), its OpenVPN-based remote-access service: versions 1.0.0 to 4.2.0 accept configuration supplied by the server without proper certificate validation, so an attacker on the network path could impersonate the server. Version 4.2.2 fixes it and is available through Moxa support. The same advisory covers the OnCell G3150A-LTE cellular gateway: CVE-2026-111460 (7.7) is a set of static HTTPS and CA private keys in its firmware, and CVE-2026-111461 (7.5) lets a privileged remote attacker inject commands through SMS management when that feature is enabled. Moxa considers the gateway end-of-life and will not fix it; its mitigations are to reset the device so it generates new keys and to keep SMS management disabled, as it is by default. No exploitation has been reported. Cellular gateways like this often link remote substations, reclosers and DER sites, and vendor remote-access clients are a common route to field devices (editorial assessment). - Moxa security advisory MPSA-269510, 27 Oct 2026 (primary); CVE records via CIRCL; CERT-FR CERTFR-2026-AVI-1393 - Published 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] ABB’s PCM600 relay-engineering tool has two local flaws and no fixed version yet, only configuration workarounds
item.category: Advisory — Protection-relay engineering software, local privilege escalation, no fixed version
item.description: CISA published advisory ICSA-26-274-03 on 1 October for ABB’s Protection and Control IED Manager PCM600, versions 2.14 and earlier; ABB’s own advisories are dated 28 September. CVE-2026-15952 (CVSS v3.1 6.4, v4 7.1) is an incorrect permission assignment: PCM600’s Scheduler Service runs as LocalSystem while granting permissions to standard users, so an attacker with local access and valid credentials could escalate privileges. CVE-2026-15953 (v3.1 5.0, v4 5.6) is a path traversal in archive processing that could write files outside the intended directory; it needs local access and user interaction. CISA lists the Energy sector and reports no known public exploitation. ABB has released no fixed version, only mitigations. Neither flaw is remotely exploitable, but PCM600 is the tool engineers use to manage protection and control IEDs, so the workstations it runs on deserve the same care as the relays (editorial assessment). - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-274-03, 1 Oct 2026 (primary); ABB advisories 2NGA003170 and 2NGA003179, 28 Sep 2026 - ABB advisories 28 Sep 2026; CISA advisory 1 Oct 2026

item.title: [Low] CISA flags a 9.8-rated flaw in EPICS Base, the control toolkit used at accelerators and large research facilities; 7.0.11 fixes it
item.category: Advisory — Open-source research control-system toolkit, network-reachable memory flaws, no known exploitation
item.description: CISA advisory ICSA-26-300-01, published 27 October, covers EPICS Base 7.0.10 and earlier, the open-source toolkit used to build control systems at particle accelerators and other large research facilities. CVE-2026-114595 (CVSS v3.1 9.8, v4.0 9.3) is an integer overflow in network request processing that could lead to memory corruption and possibly code execution; CVE-2026-114596 (v3.1 8.2) can cause an out-of-bounds write, and CVE-2026-114597 and CVE-2026-114598 (v3.1 7.5 each) are buffer over-reads. EPICS Base 7.0.11 fixes all four. CISA reports no known exploitation but rates the flaws automatable, and lists Critical Manufacturing as the sector. Utilities are unlikely to run EPICS; it matters mainly to readers at national laboratories and energy-research sites (editorial assessment). - CISA ICS advisory ICSA-26-300-01, 27 Oct 2026 (primary); CVE records via CIRCL - Published 27 Oct 2026

item.title: [Medium] FERC staff CIP audit lessons: late-registered new generation, aggregated low-impact control and AI tools inside CIP networks
item.category: Regulation — FERC staff report on lessons learned from FY2026 CIP audits
item.description: On 13 October FERC’s Office of Electric Reliability published a staff report on lessons from its fiscal-2026 CIP audits. Most cybersecurity processes reviewed met the mandatory standards, but auditors found three recurring gaps. Some owners registered new generation late, or had not categorized BES Cyber Systems under CIP-002-5.1a, including inverter-based resources already synchronized and above the threshold; staff traces this to misreading the Commercial Operation Date, and one entity delayed registration for more than a year. In two scenarios, low-impact systems controlled by a non-registered parent over affiliated operators, or by one contractor serving several unaffiliated operators, met medium-impact criteria once their combined control was counted. And entities are bringing what the report calls super intelligence (SI) tools, such as chatbots, assistants and automated analytics, into CIP-networked environments; most had applied controls, but practices varied, and staff warns such tools can open unexpected lateral-movement or access paths. The report is non-binding; it suggests NERC consider more guidance or changes to standards or registration. - FERC news release and staff report Lessons Learned from Commission-Led CIP Reliability Audits (primary); reported by Industrial Cyber, 15 Oct - Released 13 Oct 2026

item.title: [Info] CISA’s 2030 strategy names OT asset visibility and intrusion detection as priorities and starts a review of its core services within 60 days
item.category: Policy — CISA four-year strategy; OT security named as a priority
item.description: CISA released “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail” on 26 October, a four-year strategic plan introduced by Acting Director Nick Andersen. It commits the agency to help critical-infrastructure operators improve OT security, including asset visibility and intrusion detection, and to focus resources where they will have the greatest effect, informed by infrastructure assessments that include a UK-style national risk register. CISA will begin reviewing its core services and capabilities within 60 days, complete an implementation plan with success metrics within 180 days, and report on progress after a year. The plan creates no new obligations for operators, and the coverage reviewed does not single out the electric sector. For utilities, the practical question is which CISA services they rely on today and how the service review changes them (editorial assessment). - CISA strategy “CISA 2030: Defend, Harden, Prevail”, 26 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by Cybersecurity Dive and CyberScoop, 26 Oct 2026 - Released 26 Oct 2026; service review to begin within 60 days

item.title: [Info] Accenture, Dragos and SANS launch a foundation offering free OT monitoring and training to up to 500 small utilities
item.category: Program — Industry-funded OT monitoring, deployment and training for small utilities
item.description: Accenture, Dragos and the SANS Institute announced the Community Cyber Resilience Foundation on 20 October, a nonprofit backed by about $10 million in initial funding and services, with Elastic providing technology support. Its first phase covers up to 500 utilities with annual revenue under $100 million: electric, natural-gas, water and wastewater utilities in the US (the foundation’s site also mentions Canada). Participants get the Dragos Platform, Neighborhood Keeper and OT-CERT; assessment, deployment, configuration and ongoing support from Accenture; SANS OnDemand training with GIAC certification; and hardware funding where needed, at no cost. The program adds to the more than 100 utilities already in Dragos’s Community Defense Program. The Record reports that the companies say the revenue threshold covers 97% of utilities, and that no government agency is involved. Enrollment “opens soon”, according to the foundation, which is taking names for an interest list. For cooperatives and municipal utilities it sits alongside DOE’s RMUC technical-assistance partnership in this section (editorial assessment). - Dragos announcement and Community Cyber Resilience Foundation site, 20 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by The Record and Industrial Cyber, 21 Oct 2026 - Announced 20 Oct 2026; enrollment not yet open

item.title: [Info] DOE launches a $100 million cybersecurity technical-assistance partnership for cooperative, municipal and small electric utilities
item.category: Policy — DOE cybersecurity technical assistance for small electric utilities
item.description: DOE’s Office of Cybersecurity, Energy Security, and Emergency Response (CESER) announced on 1 October the $100 million Rural and Municipal Utility Cybersecurity (RMUC) Advanced Cybersecurity Technical Assistance partnership, administered by DOE’s partnership intermediary ConnectWerx. Applicant organizations must have formal partnerships with at least six qualifying electric utilities: cooperatives, municipal utilities or small investor-owned utilities. Funded work covers assessments and planning, workforce training and certification, exercises, tool implementation, verification and validation, and threat-information sharing. DOE’s announcement gives no application deadline and points applicants to ConnectWerx for details. It creates no new requirement, but for utilities without in-house OT security staff it is a route to outside assessment and exercise help. - DOE CESER announcement, 1 Oct 2026 (primary); reported by Industrial Cyber - Announced 1 Oct 2026; no application deadline stated

item.title: [Info] CISA’s CIRCIA incident-reporting final rule is under White House review; reporting duties start only once it is published
item.category: Policy — Federal cyber incident-reporting rule under White House review
item.description: The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs logged receipt of CISA’s final Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act rule (RIN 1670-AA04) on 1 October, starting the review that comes before publication. The rule text is not public, so its final scope and definitions are not yet known. The statute calls for reporting covered cyber incidents within 72 hours and ransom payments within 24 hours, but those duties begin only on dates the final rule sets. The statutory deadline passed in October 2025 and CISA’s later targets slipped; HIPAA Journal reports publication is expected before year-end; no publication had been reported as of 28 October. Power-sector participants in a GAO roundtable released 28 September already cited overlapping reporting rules, including NERC CIP, and every participant named the forthcoming CIRCIA rule as a concern. - OIRA EO 12866 review record for RIN 1670-AA04 (primary); reported by HIPAA Journal and Paubox; GAO-26-109197 reported by Cybersecurity Dive - Received for review 1 Oct 2026; no effective date yet
